pyqs.question_text: State and prove Bernoulli's theorem for streamline flow of an incompressible fluid. Discuss two practical applications of the theorem.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Award marks for a clean derivation starting from the work-energy theorem applied to a fluid element, correct statement of the assumptions (incompressible, non-viscous, streamline flow), and the final relation between pressure, kinetic and potential energy terms per unit volume. Two correctly explained applications (e.g. venturimeter, aerofoil lift) each carry partial credit; a diagram is expected for full marks.

pyqs.question_text: Derive the Lorentz transformation equations from the postulates of special relativity and show that they reduce to the Galilean transformation when the relative velocity is much smaller than the speed of light.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Full marks require a statement of both postulates, a coordinate-geometry or algebraic derivation of the transformation equations, and an explicit limiting argument (v/c to zero) showing recovery of Galilean relations. Partial credit for stating length contraction and time dilation as corollaries without a full derivation.

pyqs.question_text: Starting from Maxwell's equations in free space, derive the wave equation for the electric field and show that electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Requires correct statement of Maxwell's four equations in vacuum, the curl-of-curl manipulation leading to the wave equation, and identification of the wave speed as 1 over the square root of mu-zero epsilon-zero, matched to the measured value of c. Marks deducted for sign errors or missing vector identities.

pyqs.question_text: Deduce Planck's radiation law for black body radiation and show how it leads to Wien's displacement law and the Rayleigh-Jeans law as limiting cases.
node_titles: Black Body Radiation and Planck's Law
pyqs.marking_scheme: Expects the quantised-oscillator argument leading to Planck's formula, correct short-wavelength limit giving Wien's law and long-wavelength limit giving Rayleigh-Jeans, with the ultraviolet catastrophe mentioned as the historical motivation. Marks for graph or curve description are a bonus, not compulsory.

pyqs.question_text: Describe the construction and working of a Michelson interferometer and explain how it can be used to determine the wavelength of monochromatic light.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Diagram of the interferometer with beam-splitter and two mirrors is essential. Explanation must connect fringe shift on mirror movement to path-difference change and derive wavelength from the number of fringes counted over a known mirror displacement. Marks lost for omitting the compensating plate's role.

pyqs.question_text: Set up the time-independent Schroedinger equation for a particle in a one-dimensional infinite potential well and obtain the allowed energy eigenvalues and normalised eigenfunctions.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Full solution requires the general solution inside the well, application of boundary conditions at both walls, quantisation of the wave number, the resulting discrete energy spectrum, and correct normalisation constant. Sketching the first two or three eigenfunctions earns extra credit.

pyqs.question_text: Explain the vector atom model and distinguish between L-S coupling and j-j coupling schemes with reference to the spectra of light and heavy atoms.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer should define orbital, spin and total angular momentum vectors, explain how they combine differently under L-S and j-j coupling, and state why L-S coupling suits lighter atoms while j-j coupling suits heavier atoms with strong spin-orbit interaction. Term symbol notation earns extra marks.

pyqs.question_text: Discuss the semi-empirical mass formula for nuclear binding energy and explain the physical origin of each of its terms.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Each of the volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry and pairing terms must be named with correct physical justification (short-range saturation of nuclear force, surface deficit, Coulomb repulsion, neutron-proton asymmetry, and pairing of like nucleons). Marks for stating the formula's use in predicting the stability valley.

pyqs.question_text: Explain the liquid drop model and the shell model of the nucleus. Bring out the evidence that supports the shell model over the liquid drop model for certain nuclei.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer must contrast the collective, charged-liquid-drop picture with the independent-particle shell picture, cite magic numbers as evidence for shell closure, and note that neither model alone explains all nuclear properties. Marks for a balanced comparison rather than describing only one model.

pyqs.question_text: Derive Bragg's law of X-ray diffraction from a crystal lattice and describe how the powder diffraction method is used to determine the structure of a simple cubic crystal.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Derivation must use path-difference geometry between successive lattice planes to obtain n-lambda equals 2d-sin-theta. Description of the powder method should mention random crystallite orientation, cone of diffracted rays, and use of the Bragg angle to back out interplanar spacing and lattice parameter.

pyqs.question_text: Explain the BCS theory of superconductivity in outline and describe the Meissner effect.
node_titles: Band Theory of Solids and Superconductivity
pyqs.marking_scheme: Outline must mention Cooper pair formation via phonon-mediated attraction, the energy gap at the Fermi surface, and zero resistance below the critical temperature. The Meissner effect answer should describe expulsion of magnetic flux and distinguish a superconductor from a perfect conductor.

pyqs.question_text: Draw the circuit of an NPN transistor connected as a common-emitter amplifier and explain its working, including the roles of biasing and the coupling capacitors.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Correct circuit diagram with base, collector and emitter resistors, biasing arrangement and coupling capacitors is compulsory. Explanation must cover current amplification, the 180-degree phase reversal of output with respect to input, and the purpose of the bypass capacitor across the emitter resistor.

pyqs.question_text: Simplify the Boolean expression using De Morgan's laws and realise the simplified expression using NAND gates only.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Marks for correct application of De Morgan's identities to reduce the expression to its simplest sum-of-products or product-of-sums form, followed by a correctly drawn NAND-only realisation. Partial credit for a correct simplification even if the gate-level diagram has minor errors.

pyqs.question_text: Explain the physical origin of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and illustrate it with the example of a single-slit diffraction experiment.
pyqs.marking_scheme: Answer should state the uncertainty relation between position and momentum, explain that it is a fundamental feature of wave-particle duality rather than a measurement limitation, and connect slit width to momentum spread using the single-slit diffraction pattern as a worked illustration.

content_items.title: Particle and Rigid Body Mechanics: From Newton's Laws to Euler's Equations
content_items.body: Classical mechanics begins with Newton's three laws, which together fix how a particle's momentum changes under an applied force and guarantee that momentum and energy are conserved in an isolated system. When a system experiences only a central force, one whose magnitude depends solely on the separation between two bodies and is directed along the line joining them, angular momentum about the force centre is automatically conserved because the force can exert no torque about that point. This single fact explains why planetary orbits are planar and why Kepler's second law, equal areas swept in equal times, follows directly from angular momentum conservation rather than needing to be assumed separately. Reducing the two-body problem, such as a planet orbiting the Sun, to an equivalent one-body problem is achieved by introducing the reduced mass, which lets the relative motion of the pair be treated as a single fictitious particle moving under the combined central force. This trick considerably simplifies deriving Kepler's first law, that orbits are conic sections, and his third law relating the orbital period to the semi-major axis. Moving from point particles to extended rigid bodies introduces rotational dynamics, where the key idea is that a rigid body's orientation in three dimensions needs three independent angles, commonly chosen as the Euler angles, to specify fully. The moment of inertia tensor replaces the single scalar mass of particle mechanics, and its principal axes are the directions along which rotation produces angular momentum parallel to the angular velocity itself, avoiding the complication of precession for torque-free motion about those axes. Euler's equations of rigid body motion describe how the angular velocity components along the principal axes evolve under applied torques, and they explain phenomena that have no analogue in particle mechanics, such as the tumbling instability of a rotating object thrown into the air when spun about its intermediate principal axis, and the steady precession of a spinning top or gyroscope under gravity. The gyroscope's resistance to changing its spin axis, and its tendency to precess perpendicular to an applied torque rather than tip over, is a direct and often counter-intuitive consequence of angular momentum being a vector quantity that changes only in the direction of the applied torque. Molecular rotational motion, treated quantum mechanically in spectroscopy, still borrows the classical moment-of-inertia framework to interpret rotational energy levels. Together, these ideas, conservation laws, central force reduction, and rigid body rotation, form the conceptual backbone that later mechanics topics, including the continuum mechanics of elastic solids and fluids, build upon by treating matter as a collection of infinitesimal mass elements obeying the same underlying Newtonian framework.

Central Forces and the Two-Body Problem

content_items.title: Elasticity, Viscosity and Bernoulli's Principle in Continuous Media
content_items.body: When matter is treated as a continuous medium rather than a collection of discrete particles, the mechanics of deformable solids and fluids can be built from a small set of empirical relations that connect applied stress to resulting strain or flow. For an isotropic elastic solid obeying Hooke's law, stress is proportional to strain within the elastic limit, and the proportionality constants, Young's modulus, the bulk modulus and the modulus of rigidity, together with Poisson's ratio, are not independent; any two of them fix the rest, because they all describe the same underlying atomic bonding through different loading geometries. Young's modulus characterises resistance to stretching along one axis, the bulk modulus characterises resistance to uniform volume compression, and the modulus of rigidity characterises resistance to shape-distorting shear. Poisson's ratio quantifies how much a material contracts sideways when stretched lengthwise, a purely geometric consequence of volume being nearly conserved during elastic deformation in most solids. Moving to fluids, viscosity is the internal friction that resists relative sliding between adjacent fluid layers, and Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress between layers is proportional to the velocity gradient perpendicular to the flow, with the constant of proportionality being the coefficient of viscosity. This idea underlies Poiseuille's analysis of flow through a narrow tube, where the parabolic velocity profile arises because the fluid layer touching the tube wall is stationary while the centre moves fastest, and the volume flow rate depends on the fourth power of the tube radius, making even small changes in vessel diameter dramatically affect flow, a fact with direct relevance to blood flow in physiology. Bernoulli's theorem, derived from the work-energy theorem applied to a streamline of an ideal, incompressible, non-viscous fluid in steady flow, states that the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume remains constant along that streamline. A direct consequence is that fluid speeding up through a constriction must experience a corresponding pressure drop, the principle exploited by a venturimeter to measure flow rate and by an aerofoil, where the curved upper surface causes air to travel faster and thus at lower pressure than the flatter underside, generating lift. Real fluids depart from this ideal picture because viscosity dissipates energy, which is why practical pipe-flow calculations must add a friction-loss term to the ideal Bernoulli equation. Together, elasticity and fluid dynamics show how a handful of linear response laws, valid only for small deformations or slow, viscous-dominated flows, can be extended into powerful predictive tools across engineering and the natural sciences.

content_items.title: Special Relativity: Postulates, Lorentz Transformations and Mass-Energy Equivalence
content_items.body: Special relativity grew out of a puzzle exposed by the Michelson-Morley experiment, which tried and failed to detect the motion of the Earth through a hypothesised luminiferous ether by measuring tiny differences in the speed of light along perpendicular directions. The null result suggested that light travels at the same speed in every inertial frame, regardless of the observer's motion, a conclusion that clashed with the everyday, Galilean expectation that velocities simply add. Einstein resolved the conflict by elevating two ideas to postulates: that the laws of physics take the same form in every inertial frame, and that the speed of light in vacuum is the same constant for all inertial observers. From these two statements alone, the Lorentz transformation equations can be derived, replacing the Galilean transformation's simple addition of coordinates with equations that mix space and time coordinates together, weighted by a factor commonly denoted gamma that grows without bound as relative velocity approaches the speed of light. Two immediate and experimentally verified consequences follow. Length contraction says that an object's measured length along its direction of motion shrinks, as seen by an observer relative to whom it is moving, while its rest-frame length is unaffected. Time dilation says that a clock moving relative to an observer appears to tick more slowly than an identical clock at rest with that observer, an effect confirmed by the longer apparent lifetimes of fast-moving unstable particles such as muons produced in the upper atmosphere and detected at ground level in greater numbers than non-relativistic decay rates would predict. Velocity addition also changes: two velocities that would simply add in Galilean mechanics instead combine through a relativistic formula that ensures no combination of sub-light velocities can ever produce a resultant velocity exceeding the speed of light. Perhaps the most famous consequence is the mass-energy relation, which shows that a body's rest mass is itself a form of stored energy, released or absorbed whenever the body's internal state changes, as in nuclear reactions. This relation emerges naturally once energy and momentum are combined into a four-vector whose invariant length, unchanged under Lorentz transformation, equals rest mass times the speed of light squared. The four-momentum formalism reframes the conservation of energy and the conservation of momentum as two components of a single, frame-independent conservation law, an elegant unification that becomes indispensable in particle physics, where reactions must respect this combined conservation law when particles are created or destroyed at speeds close to that of light.

content_items.title: Interference, Diffraction and the Michelson Interferometer
content_items.body: Wave optics explains phenomena that geometrical, ray-based optics cannot, because it treats light as a wave capable of superposing with itself. Young's double-slit experiment is the clearest demonstration: light from a single source, split into two coherent secondary sources by narrow slits, produces alternating bright and dark fringes on a screen wherever the path difference between the two waves is, respectively, a whole number or a half-integer number of wavelengths. The fringe spacing depends on the wavelength of light, the slit separation and the screen distance, which is precisely why the experiment can be used, in reverse, to measure an unknown wavelength once the geometry is known. Diffraction extends this idea to a single aperture or an obstacle, showing that light bends around edges and produces its own characteristic pattern of bright and dark regions, a central bright maximum flanked by progressively weaker side maxima for a single slit. A diffraction grating, consisting of thousands of closely and regularly spaced slits, sharpens this pattern into narrow, well-separated principal maxima whose angular positions depend sensitively on wavelength, making the grating an effective tool for resolving closely spaced spectral lines, a task at which a simple prism is far less precise. Polarisation reveals a further wave property unique to transverse waves: unpolarised light, whose electric field vibrates in all directions perpendicular to its propagation, can be filtered by a polarising material to vibrate along a single direction, and the transmitted intensity through a second polariser varies with the cosine-squared of the angle between the two polarising axes, a relation known as Malus's law. The Michelson interferometer applies the interference principle in an instrument of great practical importance. A beam splitter divides incoming light into two paths, each reflected back by a mirror, one of which can be moved with extremely fine control; the recombined beams interfere constructively or destructively depending on the path difference between the two arms. As the movable mirror is displaced, the observer sees the fringe pattern shift, and counting a known number of fringe shifts for a measured mirror displacement allows the wavelength of the light source to be calculated with high precision. A compensating plate matching the beam-splitter's thickness is included in one arm to ensure both light paths pass through equal amounts of glass, eliminating a spurious path-difference contribution from dispersion. Historically, this same instrument, in the hands of Michelson and Morley, was used to search for the ether drift, and its null result became one of the pillars motivating special relativity, linking wave optics directly to the foundations of modern physics.

content_items.title: Maxwell's Equations and the Electromagnetic Wave
content_items.body: James Clerk Maxwell's great achievement was to notice that the equations describing electric and magnetic fields, as understood from Coulomb's law, Gauss's law for magnetism, Faraday's law of induction and Ampere's circuital law, were mutually inconsistent unless one additional term was added. Ampere's law related the circulating magnetic field around a wire to the electric current it carried, but this law failed for a charging capacitor, where current does not physically flow between the plates yet a magnetic field is still observed. Maxwell resolved the inconsistency by introducing the displacement current, proportional to the rate of change of the electric field between the plates, which restores consistency across every possible circuit configuration. With this correction, the four equations, now called Maxwell's equations, form a complete and symmetric description of how electric and magnetic fields are generated by charges, currents and by each other's time variation. Taking the curl of Faraday's law and substituting the corrected Ampere's law into it produces, after some vector algebra, a wave equation for the electric field in free space, with an identical equation following for the magnetic field. The speed that emerges from this derivation depends only on two constants measured in entirely separate contexts, the permittivity and permeability of free space, and its numerical value matches the independently measured speed of light so closely that Maxwell himself concluded light must itself be an electromagnetic wave, unifying optics with electricity and magnetism in one stroke. The resulting wave has its electric and magnetic field vectors oscillating perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, making it a transverse wave, and the Poynting vector, formed from the cross product of the electric and magnetic fields, gives both the direction and the rate of energy flow carried by the wave. This energy-flow description explains how electromagnetic waves can transport power across empty space, from radio transmission to sunlight warming the Earth, without any material medium carrying the energy. Boundary conditions at the interface between two different media, requiring continuity of the tangential electric field and of the normal component of the magnetic flux density, explain reflection and refraction of electromagnetic waves in terms of the same underlying field equations, connecting the wave theory back to the ray-based laws of geometrical optics as a high-frequency limiting case. Maxwell's synthesis thus stands as one of the most consequential unifications in physics, reducing electricity, magnetism and optics to a single coherent framework.

content_items.title: Black Body Radiation and the Birth of Quantum Theory
content_items.body: A black body is an idealised object that absorbs all radiation falling on it and, when in thermal equilibrium, re-emits energy across a continuous spectrum of wavelengths whose distribution depends only on its temperature. Late nineteenth-century physicists tried to explain this spectrum using classical electromagnetic theory and statistical mechanics, treating the radiation inside a cavity as a collection of standing electromagnetic waves, each mode able to absorb an arbitrary, continuously variable amount of energy. This approach, formalised in the Rayleigh-Jeans law, matched observations reasonably well at long wavelengths but predicted that the energy radiated should increase without bound as wavelength decreased, an absurd result at odds with experiment that came to be called the ultraviolet catastrophe, since no real black body radiates infinite energy in the ultraviolet region. Max Planck resolved this contradiction with a bold and, at the time, purely mathematical assumption: that the energy exchanged between the cavity walls and the electromagnetic field could only occur in discrete packets, or quanta, whose size is proportional to the frequency of the radiation, with the proportionality constant now known as Planck's constant. Treating the oscillators lining the cavity walls as restricted to this discrete ladder of energy levels, and applying the standard statistical mechanics of thermal equilibrium, Planck derived a radiation formula that matched the observed black body spectrum at every wavelength and temperature. At long wavelengths, where the energy quantum is small compared to the available thermal energy, Planck's formula smoothly reduces to the classical Rayleigh-Jeans result, showing that classical physics was not wrong so much as an approximation valid only in that limit. At short wavelengths, the discreteness of energy exchange becomes decisive: because emitting or absorbing even a single quantum requires more energy than is typically available, the probability of emission is exponentially suppressed, which is exactly the behaviour captured by Wien's law and which naturally avoids the ultraviolet catastrophe. Wien's displacement law, which states that the wavelength of peak emission shifts inversely with temperature, and Stefan's law, which states that the total radiated power grows with the fourth power of temperature, both fall out of Planck's formula as special cases, unifying several previously separate empirical laws under one theoretical roof. Beyond resolving a specific experimental puzzle, Planck's quantum hypothesis planted the seed for an entirely new physics, since Einstein later used the same idea of energy quanta to explain the photoelectric effect, and within three decades this single assumption had grown into the full formalism of quantum mechanics.

content_items.title: Laws of Thermodynamics, Entropy and Statistical Distributions
content_items.body: Thermodynamics describes energy exchange in bulk matter using a small number of state functions and empirical laws, while statistical physics explains why those laws hold by counting the microscopic arrangements available to a system. The zeroth law establishes that temperature is a well-defined quantity by asserting that two systems each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. The first law is simply energy conservation applied to heat and work, stating that the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added minus the work done by the system. The second law introduces entropy, a state function that never decreases for an isolated system undergoing any real process, and it explains why certain processes, such as heat flowing spontaneously from hot to cold but never the reverse, are irreversible even though they would not violate energy conservation if they ran backward. Carnot's analysis of an idealised, reversible heat engine operating between two temperature reservoirs sets an absolute upper limit on the efficiency any real engine can achieve, a limit that depends only on the two reservoir temperatures and not on the working substance, and every real engine cycle, whether Otto, Diesel or Rankine, is judged against this Carnot benchmark. The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches a constant, often taken as zero, as temperature approaches absolute zero, effectively ruling out ever reaching absolute zero in a finite number of steps. Statistical physics gives entropy a microscopic meaning: it is proportional to the logarithm of the number of microscopic arrangements, or microstates, consistent with a system's observed macroscopic state, so the second law simply reflects the overwhelming statistical likelihood of evolving toward the macrostate with the largest number of available microstates. Three distribution laws describe how particles occupy energy states depending on their quantum statistics. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution applies to classical, distinguishable particles such as molecules in an ideal gas, and it underlies the derivation of gas pressure, the Maxwell speed distribution, and the equipartition of energy among translational, rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom. The Bose-Einstein distribution applies to indistinguishable particles with integer spin, called bosons, which can occupy the same quantum state without restriction, a fact that explains phenomena such as Bose-Einstein condensation and the statistics underlying black body radiation itself, since photons are bosons. The Fermi-Dirac distribution applies to indistinguishable half-integer spin particles, called fermions, which obey the Pauli exclusion principle forbidding two identical fermions from occupying the same quantum state, and this single restriction explains the structure of the periodic table, the behaviour of conduction electrons in metals, and the pressure that supports white dwarf stars against gravitational collapse.

content_items.title: The Schroedinger Equation and Quantum Systems
content_items.body: Quantum mechanics departs from classical physics by describing a particle not through a definite trajectory but through a wavefunction, a complex-valued function whose squared magnitude gives the probability density of finding the particle at a given position and time. The time-dependent Schroedinger equation governs how this wavefunction evolves, playing a role analogous to Newton's second law in classical mechanics but built around the Hamiltonian operator, representing total energy, acting on the wavefunction. When the potential energy does not change with time, the equation separates into a spatial part, the time-independent Schroedinger equation, and a simple oscillating time factor, and solving the spatial equation for a given potential yields both the allowed energy eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions. The particle in an infinite one-dimensional potential well is the simplest non-trivial example: since the wavefunction must vanish at the impenetrable walls, only certain standing-wave solutions fit inside the well, producing a discrete ladder of allowed energies that grow with the square of an integer quantum number, in sharp contrast to the continuous range of energies a classical particle could have in the same box. This discreteness, an inevitable consequence of confining a wave to a finite region, recurs throughout quantum systems, from electrons bound in atoms to particles trapped in semiconductor quantum wells. The finite potential well, where the walls have finite rather than infinite height, introduces the additional phenomenon of quantum tunnelling: the wavefunction does not vanish abruptly at the walls but decays exponentially into the classically forbidden region, giving a real, calculable probability that a particle can be found, however briefly, where classical mechanics would insist it cannot go, an effect exploited in devices such as the tunnel diode and in explaining alpha-particle decay from atomic nuclei. The quantum harmonic oscillator, another exactly solvable potential, produces evenly spaced energy levels and importantly predicts a non-zero minimum energy, the zero-point energy, even in the lowest possible state, a direct consequence of the uncertainty principle forbidding a particle from having both exactly zero position spread and exactly zero momentum spread simultaneously. This uncertainty principle, which states that the product of the uncertainties in a particle's position and momentum can never fall below a fixed minimum set by Planck's constant, is not a statement about measurement clumsiness but a fundamental feature of any wave-like description of matter, and it can be illustrated concretely by passing particles through a narrowing single slit, where squeezing the position uncertainty by narrowing the slit necessarily broadens the diffraction pattern, reflecting a corresponding increase in momentum uncertainty transverse to the beam.

content_items.title: Atomic Spectra: Coupling Schemes and the Zeeman Effect
content_items.body: The vector atom model extends the simple Bohr picture of electrons in fixed circular orbits by treating each electron's orbital and spin angular momenta as vectors that combine according to definite quantum mechanical rules to give the total angular momentum of the atom. In atoms with more than one valence electron, two limiting coupling schemes describe how these individual angular momenta add together. In L-S coupling, also called Russell-Saunders coupling, the orbital angular momenta of all the electrons first combine to give a total orbital angular momentum, and separately the individual spins combine to give a total spin, after which these two resultants couple together, weakly, through spin-orbit interaction, to give the atom's total angular momentum. This scheme works well for lighter atoms, where the electrostatic repulsion between electrons is much stronger than the relatively weak spin-orbit interaction of any individual electron, so it makes sense to add up all the orbital momenta and all the spins before considering the weaker coupling between the two sums. In j-j coupling, appropriate for heavier atoms where spin-orbit interaction for each electron becomes comparable to or stronger than the electrostatic repulsion between electrons, each electron's own orbital and spin angular momenta combine first into an individual total angular momentum, and only afterward do these individual totals combine to give the atom's overall angular momentum. The resulting energy level structure, and the allowed transitions between levels that give rise to observed spectral lines, differ characteristically between the two schemes, and spectroscopists use term symbols, a compact notation recording the total spin, orbital and total angular momentum quantum numbers, to label these levels. The Zeeman effect provides a further probe of atomic structure: when an atom is placed in an external magnetic field, its energy levels split according to the projection of angular momentum along the field direction, and transitions between the split levels produce a spectral line that splits into several closely spaced components. The normal Zeeman effect, seen in atoms whose net spin is zero, splits each line into three components with a spacing set by the applied field strength and fundamental constants. The anomalous Zeeman effect, seen in atoms with non-zero net spin, produces a more complex splitting pattern that puzzled physicists until the discovery of electron spin explained it as arising from the different magnetic moment associated with spin compared to orbital motion, a discrepancy captured by the Lande g-factor. Together, coupling schemes and the Zeeman effect illustrate how the fine details of atomic spectra encode deep information about how angular momentum and magnetism operate at the quantum level.

content_items.title: Nuclear Models: The Liquid Drop and Shell Pictures
content_items.body: Understanding how protons and neutrons bind together inside the atomic nucleus requires balancing two very different theoretical pictures, each capturing part of the truth. The liquid drop model treats the nucleus as an incompressible drop of nuclear fluid, where each nucleon interacts only with its immediate neighbours because the strong nuclear force has an extremely short range, much like the short-range forces between molecules in a liquid. This analogy leads directly to the semi-empirical mass formula, which expresses the total binding energy of a nucleus as a sum of terms: a volume term proportional to the number of nucleons, reflecting the short-range saturation of the nuclear force; a surface term that subtracts binding energy because nucleons at the nuclear surface have fewer neighbours than those deep inside, exactly as surface tension reduces a liquid drop's stability; a Coulomb term that subtracts energy due to electrostatic repulsion among protons; an asymmetry term that penalises nuclei with very unequal numbers of protons and neutrons, reflecting the quantum mechanical tendency of nucleons to fill energy levels most efficiently when the two numbers are close; and a pairing term that adds extra stability to nuclei with even numbers of protons and neutrons, since like nucleons prefer to pair up with opposite spins. This formula successfully predicts the overall trend of binding energy per nucleon across the periodic table, including the peak around iron and nickel that explains why fusion releases energy for light elements while fission releases energy for heavy ones. However, the liquid drop model fails to explain certain sharp irregularities, most notably the unusual stability of nuclei with specific numbers of protons or neutrons, called magic numbers, which show binding energies distinctly higher than the smooth liquid-drop trend would predict. The shell model resolves this by treating each nucleon as moving independently in an average potential well created by all the other nucleons, filling discrete energy levels much as electrons fill shells in an atom, and a strong spin-orbit coupling term, much larger than its atomic counterpart, correctly reproduces the observed magic numbers as points where a major shell closes. Nuclei with closed shells are more tightly bound and more resistant to further nucleon addition, mirroring the chemical inertness of noble gases with closed electron shells. Neither model is complete on its own: the liquid drop model excels at describing collective properties, average binding energy and the mechanics of fission, while the shell model excels at explaining individual nuclear spins, magnetic moments and the special stability of magic-number nuclei, and modern nuclear theory often combines both pictures in a unified collective model.

content_items.title: Nuclear Fission, Fusion and the Building Blocks of Matter
content_items.body: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus, typically uranium or plutonium, into two lighter fragments accompanied by the release of two or three neutrons and a substantial amount of energy. The process can be understood through the liquid drop model: absorbing a neutron excites the nucleus into oscillation, and if the resulting deformation stretches the nuclear drop enough that the disruptive Coulomb repulsion between protons overcomes the attractive surface tension holding the drop together, the nucleus splits at the narrow neck of the deformed shape. The released neutrons can go on to induce fission in neighbouring nuclei, creating the possibility of a self-sustaining chain reaction, controlled in a nuclear reactor by materials that absorb excess neutrons and uncontrolled in a fission weapon. Nuclear fusion works in the opposite direction, combining two light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen, into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy because the binding energy per nucleon of the heavier product exceeds that of the light reactants. Fusion requires extremely high temperatures and densities to overcome the mutual Coulomb repulsion between positively charged nuclei long enough for the short-range nuclear force to bind them together, conditions naturally present in stellar cores and pursued artificially, so far without sustained net energy gain, in magnetic and inertial confinement fusion reactors on Earth. Both processes are governed by the same underlying binding-energy curve: because binding energy per nucleon peaks around iron, any nuclear rearrangement that moves lighter nuclei toward iron, fusion, or heavier nuclei toward iron, fission, releases energy, while rearrangement in the opposite direction would require an input of energy. Beta decay, a third fundamental nuclear process, converts a neutron into a proton or vice versa within the nucleus while emitting an electron or positron and an associated neutrino. Its most striking feature is parity violation, discovered through the famous cobalt-60 experiment, which showed that beta decay does not treat left and right symmetrically, a violation of a symmetry that had been assumed to hold universally in physics until that point. Beyond the nucleus itself, elementary particle physics probes the deeper structure of the particles that make up nucleons. Protons and neutrons are not fundamental but are composed of quarks, elementary particles carrying fractional electric charge and bound together by the strong force, mediated by particles called gluons, in a scheme that groups particles into families called hadrons, further divided into baryons made of three quarks and mesons made of a quark-antiquark pair. This quark structure, confirmed by deep inelastic scattering experiments that revealed point-like constituents inside protons, extends the reductionist programme of physics one level deeper than the nucleus, showing that nuclear physics itself rests on a still more fundamental layer of matter.

content_items.title: Crystal Structure, X-ray Diffraction and Band Theory of Solids
content_items.body: The properties of a solid depend heavily on how its constituent atoms are arranged in space, and crystallography classifies these arrangements into a small number of repeating unit cells, described by the seven crystal systems and, when the arrangement of atoms within the cell is also considered, the fourteen Bravais lattices. X-ray diffraction is the principal experimental tool for determining these structures, because X-ray wavelengths are comparable to the spacing between atomic planes in a crystal, allowing the crystal lattice to act as a natural diffraction grating. Bragg's law captures the condition for constructive interference between X-rays reflecting off successive parallel planes of atoms: the extra path length travelled by a ray reflecting off a deeper plane must equal a whole number of wavelengths, giving the relation between the X-ray wavelength, the interplanar spacing and the angle of incidence at which a strong reflected beam is observed. In the powder diffraction method, a finely powdered sample presents crystallites in every possible orientation simultaneously, so that for each family of lattice planes, some crystallites will always be oriented at exactly the Bragg angle, producing a cone of diffracted rays that intersects a detector or photographic film as a ring, or, in modern instruments, a discrete peak in a plot of intensity against angle. Measuring the angles of these peaks allows the interplanar spacings, and from them the full lattice geometry and unit cell dimensions, to be reconstructed. Once the atomic arrangement is known, band theory explains why some solids conduct electricity freely while others do not. When individual atoms are brought together to form a crystal, their discrete energy levels broaden into continuous bands of allowed energy, separated by gaps of forbidden energy, as a direct consequence of the Pauli exclusion principle preventing electrons in overlapping orbitals from sharing identical quantum states. In a conductor, the highest occupied band is only partially filled, so electrons can easily move into nearby empty states under an applied electric field, producing current. In an insulator, the highest occupied band, the valence band, is completely full and separated from the next available band, the conduction band, by a large energy gap that electrons cannot easily cross using ordinary thermal energy. A semiconductor has the same band structure as an insulator but with a much smaller gap, so a modest amount of thermal energy or an added impurity can promote enough electrons across the gap to allow appreciable, temperature-sensitive conduction, a property exploited throughout modern electronics and explored further in the physics of superconductivity, where certain materials lose all electrical resistance below a critical temperature through the pairing of electrons described by BCS theory.
node_titles: Band Theory of Solids and Superconductivity

content_items.title: Semiconductor Devices: From the p-n Junction to the Transistor Amplifier
content_items.body: A semiconductor such as silicon can be deliberately modified through doping, the controlled introduction of impurity atoms, to change its electrical behaviour in a precise and useful way. Adding a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus contributes an extra, loosely bound electron to the crystal, creating an n-type semiconductor in which negatively charged electrons are the majority charge carriers. Adding a trivalent impurity such as boron leaves a missing bond, or hole, that behaves as a mobile positive charge carrier, creating a p-type semiconductor. When a p-type and an n-type region are formed within the same crystal, the junction between them, the p-n junction, becomes the basic building block of nearly all semiconductor devices. At the junction, electrons from the n-side diffuse across to combine with holes on the p-side and vice versa, leaving behind a thin depletion region stripped of mobile charge carriers and containing an internal electric field that opposes further diffusion, establishing an equilibrium barrier potential. Applying an external voltage in the forward direction, positive terminal to the p-side, reduces this barrier and allows a large current to flow, while applying voltage in the reverse direction increases the barrier and permits only a negligible leakage current, giving the junction its essential property as a rectifier, converting alternating current into a one-directional, pulsating current. A bipolar junction transistor extends this idea by sandwiching a very thin, lightly doped middle region between two more heavily doped regions of the opposite type, forming either an NPN or PNP structure. In an NPN transistor operated as a common-emitter amplifier, the emitter-base junction is forward biased while the base-collector junction is reverse biased; the forward bias injects a large number of electrons from the emitter into the thin base region, and because the base is so thin and lightly doped, most of these electrons diffuse across it and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased junction's field rather than recombining within the base. A small change in base current therefore controls a much larger change in collector current, giving the transistor its current-amplifying ability, and because the output is taken across a collector resistor while the input is applied at the base, the output voltage swings in the opposite phase to the input voltage, producing the characteristic 180-degree phase reversal of a common-emitter stage. Coupling capacitors at the input and output block any unwanted direct-current bias from reaching adjacent stages or the source and load while still allowing the amplified alternating signal to pass through, and a bypass capacitor placed across the emitter resistor prevents the loss of gain that would otherwise occur from negative feedback introduced by that resistor at signal frequencies, while still allowing the resistor to stabilise the direct-current operating point against temperature drift.

content_items.title: Boolean Algebra, Logic Gates and the Basics of Microprocessors
content_items.body: Digital electronics represents information using only two discrete voltage levels, conventionally labelled 0 and 1, and Boolean algebra provides the mathematical framework for combining such binary signals through logical operations. The three basic operations, AND, OR and NOT, can be combined to build any more complex logical function, and a small set of algebraic identities, including the commutative, associative and distributive laws familiar from ordinary algebra, along with De Morgan's laws, allow a complicated Boolean expression to be simplified into a more economical form before it is built in hardware. De Morgan's laws state that the complement of a sum of variables equals the product of their individual complements, and the complement of a product equals the sum of their individual complements, a pair of identities that is especially useful because it allows any logical expression, however it is originally written, to be re-expressed using only NAND or only NOR operations, each of which is individually described as a universal gate capable of implementing every other logical function on its own. This universality has great practical value, because a digital circuit built entirely from one repeated type of gate is simpler and cheaper to manufacture in bulk than one requiring several different gate types. Beyond the basic gates, combinational circuits such as adders, multiplexers and decoders combine multiple gates to perform arithmetic or data-routing tasks with no memory of past inputs, while sequential circuits such as flip-flops introduce memory, allowing a circuit's output to depend on its history as well as its current input, the essential ingredient for building registers, counters and, eventually, entire computer memories. A microprocessor integrates arithmetic, logic and control circuitry onto a single chip, orchestrating the fetch-decode-execute cycle by which a stored sequence of binary instructions is read from memory, interpreted, and carried out step by step. Registers inside the microprocessor hold data and instructions temporarily during this cycle, the arithmetic logic unit performs the actual computations demanded by each instruction, and the control unit generates the timing and sequencing signals that coordinate every other component, all synchronised to a central clock signal whose frequency sets the overall processing speed. Input and output ports allow the microprocessor to communicate with external devices, while an address bus and a data bus carry, respectively, the location and the content of each piece of information being transferred to or from memory. Although modern processors have grown vastly more complex, incorporating multiple cores, cache memory hierarchies and pipelined instruction execution, the underlying logic remains built from the same basic Boolean gates and flip-flops studied at the introductory level, illustrating how a handful of simple binary switching elements can be composed, layer upon layer, into machines capable of extraordinarily sophisticated computation.
